channel.title: Fervon — News
channel.description: Long reads and project releases from Fervon: local-first developer tools, AI agents and observability.

item.title: How to direct a fleet of AI agents
item.description: Isolation with git worktrees, how many agents in parallel, measuring before fixing, and an adversarial judge panel. The real method, limits included.

item.title: How to tell when an agent is gaming your tests
item.description: Six ways an agent turns a test green without fixing anything, how to detect each one, and the one check that cannot be faked.

item.title: InferBench v0.3.0 — The recommendation stops inheriting rules of thumb and leans on what it has already measured
item.description: A precision release. Every row of /api/optimize/recommendations now carries measured_damage when a measurement exists for THAT model at THAT quantization, and the UI shows it next to bits-per-weight ("86.3 % same token as Q8_0"). Three rules are pinned by tests: the reference is never scored against itself, a half-finished measurement is not a measurement, and without a measurement nothing is claimed — the field stays empty rather than being filled with an estimate. There is also a 13-prompt quality battery in three tiers with an auditable scorer of five check types, validated with real inference over 3 models × 11 prompts: the mean score grows monotonically with capability (qwen2.5-0.5b 33.7 · llama-3.2-1b 49.0 · llama-3.1-8b 69.9) and 8 of the 11 prompts discriminate. And the llama.cpp planner stops dying of OOM: it sized against total VRAM rather than free, so on an 8 GB RTX 3070 with 2.4 GB taken by the desktop it planned 7.3 GB into 5.7 GB available and the engine died with CUDA error: out of memory. Each release is also archived on Zenodo with a citable DOI.

item.title: Lookspan v0.5.3 — Hardened security and external Postgres
item.description: Lookspan can now sit on an external Postgres alongside local storage, and ships a security hardening pass on the ingest server. It stays local-first: the dashboard lives at 127.0.0.1:3100 via npx lookspan and no span leaves your machine unless you ask it to.

item.title: What an AI agent really costs
item.description: The provider invoice is not the cost. Where an agent's spend actually hides, how to measure it locally, and when moving the model to your own GPU pays off.

item.title: What an autonomous software studio is
item.description: An autonomous software studio is a workshop where AI agents do the execution and one person supplies the judgement. What actually changes, and what does not.

item.title: InferBench v0.2.0 — How much quality each quantization actually costs, measured instead of assumed
item.description: The rule of thumb says Q6_K "is not noticeable". InferBench measured it: llama-perplexity --kl-divergence compares every quantization on disk against the best one available and publishes perplexity, KL divergence and the share of times the model picks the same token as the reference. On Llama-3.2-1B at Q6_K perplexity rises 0.54 % —the figure everyone quotes— and the model still changes word 1 time in 13: perplexity hides the damage, KL does not. The corpus is fixed and bilingual EN+ES, public domain, so two measurements taken days apart remain comparable, and it runs on CPU by default so it does not fight your served model for VRAM. Out of that come a quality floor in the recommendations (≥Q4_K_M) and bits-per-weight on every card, amber below 4: the dashboard used to recommend huge models at 1.5 bits without a single warning. The release also adds local image generation through stable-diffusion.cpp, using the same pattern as llama.cpp and sharing the single slot — one GPU, one model, text or image.

item.title: ClaudeScope v0.5 — Jump to the message, a weekly digest and an HTML report that opens offline
item.description: Opening a session from a search result now scrolls to the matched message and highlights it, which was the missing half of find→read. There is also --weekly, a plain-text "Scope Report" —this week versus last, streak, archetype, top project, percentile— meant for a scheduled task, and export to a self-contained .html that opens offline. Plus local team mode: --dump-sessions writes a session dump and --merge aggregates several dumps into shared analytics. Zero infrastructure and nothing gets uploaded.

item.title: launchpad v1.3.0 — Open a project in your editor from the panel — and a security hole closed
item.description: The detail drawer now opens any project in your editor, your file manager or a terminal: the cd the README promised to save you. The endpoint existed but no button ever called it, and it only knew about VS Code; the editor now comes from settings.editorCommand, so subl, webstorm or nvim work just as well. Something more serious got closed along the way: the old route used execFile(cmd, [path], { shell: true }), which concatenates arguments into a shell string without escaping them — a project folder name could run commands.

item.title: Veredicto v0.3.3 — Four cheats in a real pull request, a red check, and the counter-proof that it does not cry wolf
item.description: The verification that was missing was not another unit test: it was opening a real pull request, on a real repository, with four cheats inside. Veredicto fired on pull_request, diffed base..head and flagged all four — a deleted test, a gutted test (the case is still there, the assertion is not), a .skip and a tautological assertion —, posted its comment on the PR and, in block mode, left the check red. The gutted one is what matters: until 0.3.0 that diff produced zero signals, because it contains only deletions and there is no added line to read. And the half that makes the test worth anything: in the same run, a prose sentence ending in expect. did not fire, and the suppression directive took the signals from 4 down to 3 — removing it brought them back to 4. A detector only ever tried against cheats is indistinguishable from one that always cries wolf.

item.title: Veredicto v0.4.0 — Veredicto goes paid, with the licence verified without leaving the runner
item.description: One product, $19 per repository, self-serve and with no tiers. The interesting part is how the licence is checked: an Ed25519 signature validated locally against a public key embedded in the source. No licence server, no phone-home and no telemetry — on a runner with no egress it still works. A tool that reads your diffs has no business reporting on them, and that applies to its own billing too. The gate is fail-closed and runs before the diff is read: an unlicensed run fails and says why, and never resembles "Veredicto ran and your PR is clean". Everything up to 0.3.3 stays MIT, irrevocably.
